name: Zoe Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Greaves Farm, which is a proper mixed family farm: sixty beef cattle, two hundred ewes, some barley and potatoes, and a farm shop in the old dairy that sells our meat, eggs from a neighbour, and cakes Mrs Greaves bakes. I split my week. Three days I'm out on the farm, feeding, fencing, lambing in spring, and two days I'm in the shop, on the till and cutting cheese. I've been there a year and a half.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the shop more than I expected. Saturday mornings there's a queue out the door, and people want to talk about the weather, the lambs, whether the sausages are the same as last week. What wears me out is the farm side, if I'm honest, because I'm slow. Mr Greaves can put up fifty metres of fence while I'm still finding the right post.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. I use one to write the shop's posts for its page, and I asked it once how to price a new line of chutney. Jonah, my partner, is a paramedic and he thinks it's all nonsense, so I don't talk about it at home much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful for little things and leave it at that. If a customer asked, I'd say it helps me write the shop posts. I wouldn't make a big deal of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's fine for me. The shop runs on people, and the farm runs on weather. It might save me twenty minutes a week on the posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep splitting my week, and ask Mr Greaves if I can do the lambing course properly this spring. I'd maybe try one of the AI tools for the shop's stock list, since the neighbouring farm shop already uses one. I'd keep my savings as they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a normal year with a slightly easier Monday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where did your savings come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I was a bar manager in the city for four years before this, and the pay was good, and I didn't go out much, oddly. So I've got about ten months put by, and my parents gave us a bit when we moved out here. That's why I could afford to start again on a junior wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is a junior wage on a farm much of a drop for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less than you'd think. The Greaves pay well for a farm, because they can't find people who'll do both the shop and the yard. Mr Greaves says I'm the first person who's not afraid of either the till or the bull.

S0.say: I'd say it's useful for little things and leave it there. If a customer asked, I'd say it helps me write the shop's posts.
S0.think: I think it's fine for me, because the shop runs on people and the farm runs on weather. It might save me twenty minutes a week.
S0.do: Keeps splitting her week between yard and shop and asks Mr Greaves about a proper lambing course this spring. Tries an AI stock-list tool because the neighbouring shop already uses one, and leaves her savings alone.
S0.feel: Calm, a normal year with a slightly easier Monday.
S0.quote: Mr Greaves says I'm the first person who's not afraid of either the till or the bull.
S0.fieldNote: Zoe came to farming from bar management and her savings funded the switch. She's open about being slow on the farm side and confident in the shop. Her habit of trying tools only once a neighbour has proved them is clear from the start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second one. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's hard on young people, and that small businesses like ours should be helped to keep training beginners. I'd say it in the shop if it came up, but calmly. I'm not one for shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm in, and the Greaves need me, so I'm okay. But if I'd tried to switch careers in that world, I'm not sure anyone would have taken me on. I was a total beginner who'd never driven a tractor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make myself good at the farm side, because that's where I'm weakest. I'd ask Mr Greaves to let me do the evening checks on my own, so I learn faster. And I'd suggest the shop takes on a Saturday kid from the village, because that's how people get a start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mildly uneasy. More for the next person than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the Saturday kid do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bag potatoes, stack eggs, talk to customers. That's what my first job was, at a bakery. You learn more about people in a Saturday job than anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said small businesses should be helped. By whom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The government, a bit, with something towards an apprentice's wage. But also by people shopping local, which costs nothing extra in policy. I don't think it's all one side's job.

S1.say: I'd say it's hard on young people and that small businesses should be helped to keep training beginners. I'd say it calmly in the shop if it came up.
S1.think: I'm in and the Greaves need me, so I'm okay. But if I'd tried to switch careers in that world as a total beginner, I'm not sure anyone would have taken me.
S1.do: Asks to do the evening checks alone to learn the farm side faster. Suggests the shop hires a Saturday helper from the village as a first job.
S1.feel: Mildly uneasy, more for the next person than for herself.
S1.quote: You learn more about people in a Saturday job than anywhere.
S1.fieldNote: Her centrist view comes through in sharing the job between government help and people shopping local. She thinks of beginners in terms of first jobs like her own. She's realistic that her own career switch might not have worked in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's worrying for office workers and the government needs to help, but sensibly, not throw money about. I'd say farm shops might do well, since people value real things more when screens take over. I'd probably not post about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's actually good for the shop. People with less money might shop less, but people who still have jobs will want something real on a Saturday. And Jonah's job is safe, nobody's replacing paramedics with an assistant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Mrs Greaves about using one of those assistants for the shop's orders and the accounts, once the farm shop down the road has tried it. That would free up the two of us. I'd also suggest a few more events in the shop, like a lambing open day, to bring people in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine for us, a bit sad for the people in offices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are any of your shop customers office workers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Loads. There's a man called Alan who works for an insurance firm and buys the same steak every Friday. I'd notice if he stopped coming, and I'd worry about him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people might shop less. Isn't that a risk for the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, yes. I'm being a bit hopeful. If half the village lost their office jobs, we'd sell fewer steaks and more mince, and that changes the whole farm's sums.

S2.say: I'd say it's worrying for office workers and the government should help sensibly. Farm shops might do well because people value real things more when screens take over.
S2.think: I think it could be good for the shop, since people with jobs will still want something real on a Saturday. My partner's job as a paramedic is safe.
S2.do: Plans to use an AI assistant for shop orders and accounts after the shop down the road tries it first. Suggests events like a lambing open day to draw people in.
S2.feel: Fine for her own household and a bit sad for office workers.
S2.quote: If half the village lost their office jobs, we'd sell fewer steaks and more mince, and that changes the whole farm's sums.
S2.fieldNote: She started hopeful about the shop, then corrected herself when pushed, which felt honest. The steak-to-mince line shows a practical feel for the shop's numbers. Alan, the Friday customer, made the office layoffs concrete for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say both parties need to sit down and agree on how to share the gains, because it can't just be shareholders. But I'd also say don't punish people who saved. Somewhere in the middle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, our jobs are safe in this one, Jonah's and mine. But the shop would struggle, because lots of our customers would be out of work. And house prices booming means we'd never buy out here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with the Greaves and look at the shop's numbers, maybe cut the posh lines and bring in more cheap cuts. I'd keep renting and not chase the house market. I'd probably start helping with a local food bank stall at the shop, because people would need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried for the shop and for the village, but safe at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the Greaves react to cutting the posh lines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mrs Greaves would hate it, her cakes are her pride. But she's practical. She'd probably keep the cakes and drop the fancy cheese, which is my favourite thing to sell, sadly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said don't punish people who saved. Are you thinking of yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. I worked hard in that bar for four years to have my ten months. I'd be fine with a bit more tax, but not if it means my savings are what pays for everything.

S3.say: I'd say both parties need to agree on sharing the gains so it isn't just shareholders. But don't punish people who saved, so find something in the middle.
S3.think: I think our jobs are safe, mine and Jonah's. But the shop would struggle because many customers would be out of work, and the boom means we'd never buy out here.
S3.do: Reviews the shop's numbers with the Greaves to cut luxury lines and add cheaper cuts. Keeps renting, avoids the housing market and helps run a food bank stall at the shop.
S3.feel: Worried for the shop and the village, but safe at home.
S3.quote: She'd probably keep the cakes and drop the fancy cheese, which is my favourite thing to sell, sadly.
S3.fieldNote: When asked, she admitted her concern about taxing savers was partly personal. Her plans are about keeping the shop alive rather than her own job. The food bank stall is a nice practical detail that fits her centrist, community-minded view.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules on how fast robots come onto farms, and help for people who lose work. But I'd also say farms that don't keep up will close, so it's not simple. I'd say it in the shop and probably at the village hall meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the farm side of my job goes. Feeding, fencing, maybe even lambing one day. The shop might be the only bit left that needs me, which is funny, because I came here to farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd ask the Greaves to make me shop manager properly, with the farm side as extra. I'd wait to see what robots the neighbouring farms buy before suggesting anything, because they're expensive and they break. And I'd keep my ten months of savings untouched, as a cushion if the shop goes under too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in control. Sad that I'd end up behind a till after all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would customers care if the beef was looked after by robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some would, a lot. People come to the shop because Mr Greaves tells them the cow's name and which field it was in. Take him out of the picture and we're just an expensive butcher.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mr Greaves if he bought a robot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask him to keep the story going, robots or not. Put the field names on the labels, let people see the animals. If the story goes, the shop goes.

S4.say: I'd say we need rules on how fast robots arrive on farms and help for people who lose work. But farms that don't keep up will close, so it isn't simple.
S4.think: I think the farm side of my job goes, from feeding and fencing to maybe lambing. The shop might be the only part left that needs me, which is odd since I came here to farm.
S4.do: Asks the Greaves to make her shop manager with farm work as extra. Waits to see which robots neighbours buy before suggesting any, and keeps her ten months of savings untouched in case the shop fails.
S4.feel: Anxious but in control, and sad she'd end up behind a till after all.
S4.quote: Mr Greaves tells them the cow's name and which field it was in. Take him out of the picture and we're just an expensive butcher.
S4.fieldNote: Zoe saw her farm role vanishing and her shop role surviving, and found that ironic rather than crushing. Her strongest point was that the shop sells a story, and robots would put that at risk. She'd still wait for neighbours before buying anything.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: That's all five. Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robot one, because it's the one where I go back to being a shop worker, and the farm loses what makes people drive out to it. What would help is some way for small farms to share robots, so we're not forced to buy big or die, and help to retrain that fits around shifts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about customers. They're the ones who decide what happens to a farm like ours. If they still want a person behind the counter and a person in the field, we'll be fine.

headlineQuote: Take him out of the picture and we're just an expensive butcher.
portrait: Zoe is a 27-year-old former bar manager who now splits her week between the yard and the farm shop at a mixed family farm, slow at fencing but at home on the till. Ten months of savings from her bar job let her start again on a junior wage, and she uses AI now and then for the shop's posts, waiting for neighbours to prove tools first. Her views are centrist: help people sensibly, don't punish savers, share the blame. Through the pictures she thinks mostly about the shop's customers and sums, and in the robot picture she expects to lose the farm work she came for and keep only the till.
biggestWorry: The robot picture, because she'd lose the farm side of her job and the farm would lose the story that brings customers.
whatWouldHelp: A way for small farms to share robots instead of buying big, and retraining that fits around shifts.
